question.text: Consider a hydrogen-like sample of gas whose energy in the <math><msup><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></math> excited state is given by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>13.6</mn><msup><mi>Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo> </mo><mi>eV</mi></math>. When the electron makes transitions from an excited state to the ground state, the most energetic photons can have energy <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>52.224</mn><mi> </mi><mi>eV</mi></math> and the least energetic photons can have energy <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1.224</mn><mi> </mi><mi>eV</mi></math>. If the atomic number of the atom and the state of excitation are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Z</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi></math> respectively, then what is the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Z</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></math>?

solution.text:
52.224=13.6Z2 112-1n2  .....(1)

1.224=13.6z2 1n-12-1n2  .....(2)

On solving Z = 2 n = 5
Hence Z + n = 7
